paras.t: Question 02.1 was answered well with good knowledge of the term ‘endogenous factors’ and some clear links to how these contributed to the character of places.

Question 03.1 assessed students understanding of the concept of urban decentralisation and the reasons why both people and/or businesses had moved away from city centres. Students could explain economic, social and environmental reasons behind these changes and quite often used examples to help demonstrate their understanding.

Question 01.3 and 02.3 scored almost identical mean marks into low Level 2. Question 01.3 showed students had knowledge of the role of NGOs and could assess their importance in raising awareness in the protection of Antarctica.

Question 02.3 required students to assess how a person’s lived experience affects their sense of place with the two photographs of London allowing students to consider insider and outsider perspectives.

Question 02.4 had the highest mean, indicating mid-level 3 performance. Students provided detailed place knowledge to demonstrate how shifting flows of investment had an impact on the character of the place. Detroit, areas of London (Stratford, Shoreditch, Brick Lane and Docklands) and Liverpool all featured prominently as places where shifting flows of investment (both positive and negative) had changed the character of the place over time.

Question 04.5 had a mean score of over 12 and showed students had some clear knowledge and understanding of the possible impact of the changing carbon cycle on migration. Connections were drawn between increased carbon in the atmosphere, climate change, increased weather and climate related hazards, rising sea levels, impacts on agriculture, urban flooding and the possibility of climate related migration. There was evidence of good place knowledge here. Many focused on Pacific Island communities or sub-Saharan Africa.
In question 01.1 (AO1, 4 marks) a number of students misread the key terminology in the question, producing responses referring to environmental independence rather than interdependence.
In question 02.2 there was some misinterpretation of the horizontal scale showing the percentage of respondents. Some students saw these values as actual numbers of responses.
In question 05.2, many students understood the logarithmic horizontal scale; however, some did not, and as a result, their analysis was incorrect and limited to Level 1.

The human geography examination was an accessible assessment, and it enabled students to score well across each of the themes. The overall distribution of marks indicated the paper discriminated well. The more able students could show their knowledge, understanding and skills whilst the less able could still access the lower levels of the mark scheme and gain credit.

As with previous years, students had prepared for the structure of the examination and again there were very few incidences of rubric infringement. Completing all thirteen questions is a demanding task and there were relatively few papers suggesting students had run out of time.

The standard format of the paper is for students to answer questions from two compulsory core sections and one of the three options. There was a very similar pattern of marks across the three options, but Resource security continues to be the least popular choice taught by centres. Students showed that they were well prepared and that they understood how the questions align to the Assessment Objectives (AOs). Hence, there was evidence of clear geographical knowledge and understanding (AO1), appropriate application of knowledge (AO2) and some good use of geographical skills (AO3).
All question types showed evidence of good student performance.
Performance on the 4-mark questions assessing AO1 was a particular strength.

AO3 questions provide students with the opportunity to apply geographical skills of analysis and interpretation to a variety of resources presenting geographical information. Many students accessed Level 2 by demonstrating analytical skills such as identifying overall patterns and trends, data manipulation, picking out anomalies, making connections between resources, and accurately interpreting scales and legends.
In the 6- and 9-mark questions (AO1 & AO2) that used novel stimulus material there was evidence of some student confidence and clear application of knowledge and understanding.
In Section C, students chose to answer questions from the optional topics they had studied.

In Section C, each of the 9-mark questions showed mean scores of over 5.0, indicating mid-level 2 performance. Students showed knowledge and evaluation of sustainable cities, local-scale factors negatively impacting health, and the geopolitics of mineral resources.
Student responses to the extended questions (20 marks) were often well structured and presented clear arguments with effective links to case studies.
In general, there were some errors made by students on the resources questions (AO3).

Most of the 6- and 9-mark questions evidenced some good subject knowledge and application. However, students could achieve higher marks within Level 2 or 3 by making their assessments and evaluations more explicit.

The 20-mark essays did highlight some areas for improvement. When answering 20-mark questions, students were more successful when the response continued with a single line of reasoning, compared to responses that try to offer a balanced argument or approach from different angles.

4-mark questions are point marked. A mark may be awarded where a student makes a single relevant point and subsequent marks awarded (if applicable) where the student develops those points with additional knowledge.

6-mark, 9-mark and 20-mark questions are levels marked where the response is holistically marked against the assessment objectives, given a mid-level mark initially and then a fine tune mark awarded within that level.
AO1: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of places, environments, concepts, processes, interactions and change, at a variety of scales (30-40%).
AO2: Apply knowledge and understanding in different contexts to interpret, analyse and evaluate geographical information and issues (30-40%).

AO3: Use a variety of relevant quantitative, qualitative and fieldwork skills to: - investigate geographical questions and issues - interpret, analyse and evaluate data and evidence - construct arguments and draw conclusions (20-30%)
